designs.concept: The Consultant's Almanac: KnightWebstudio set like the annual report of a serious consultancy, written for a tradesman. Warm paper, deep ink and one confident blue; numbered chapters, hairline rules, a left rail for numbers and margin notes, big Fraunces numerals and dot-leader price lists carry the page, and every automation claim is paired with a small HTML/CSS figure that shows the product doing it. Light by default; a visitor whose device prefers dark (or who uses the toggle) gets a separately finished night edition.
signatureMoments: Fig. 1 in the hero: a phone on a square blue plate showing a missed call answered by an automatic text, with numbered markers and a legend, captioned as an illustration with the $750 setup price
Hero headline set one phrase per line from 1181px up (More customers, / fewer missed calls, / hours back every week in blue italic), verified at 3 lines from 1181 to 1920px
The example week as a ledger: a real table with single-hue bars, the arithmetic per row, a 140px '200' (hours a year, in this example) in the left rail and the 'not a measurement' note beside it
Three ruled figure columns (Fig. 2 to 4): lock-screen notifications, a calendar slot filling in, and one list with follow-up chips, each above its three numbered steps
Dot-leader price lists throughout (name ........ $price), including a contents list with prices at the top of the Pricing page
Pricing tiers as four ruled columns whose price, plan, facts and buttons line up across columns via subgrid
The Launch bundle as an itemised receipt ($2,000 + $500 + $750, $3,250 struck through, $3,000) that stays sticky beside the consulting price list
Payment plan drawn to scale: a $1,000 deposit block and three 'about $333' months
The phone menu as the almanac's Contents page: numbered serif links on hairlines
The founder's note: a large first-person quote taken from the About page, signed, standing in for testimonials that do not exist yet

Fraunces Italic (variable, weight + optical size) - fraunces-italic.woff2, 81 KB

designs.concept: Show the machine working: the site demonstrates the service with small working interfaces built in HTML/CSS (a phone that misses a call, texts back, takes the reply, books the job and sends a review request; a booking calendar; a lead list) instead of describing it. Everything around those screens is kept plain and warm (paper background, ink, one blue, a highlighter stroke, ruled price lists) so a contractor reads it as a tidy work order rather than software marketing.
signatureMoments: Hero live stage: a phone plays six beats (incoming call, missed, automatic text-back, customer reply, booked on the calendar, review request) with three floating system cards; it rests in the finished picture, then rewinds and replays, with a five-stop rail to jump to any step and a pause button. Works as a static complete picture with no JavaScript or reduced motion.

Automation bento: four different tiles (notification stack for text-back, booking picker feeding a week calendar, a lead list whose status chips advance, and an inverse-coloured 'example week' ledger showing the 235-minute arithmetic with its 'not a measurement' qualifier), each demo labelled Illustration and carrying its fixed setup price.
The offer in three ruled lines inside the hero: Websites, Automation and Consulting with their fixed prices visible in the first desktop viewport.

Price sheet and payment-plan bar: the four website prices as one four-column sheet with a segmented bar drawing '50% down, then three payments'; on the pricing page, tier cards whose rows align across cards, grouped price ledgers, the Launch bundle shown as a receipt that adds up to $3,250 and lands on $3,000, and care plans as one aligned table.
Pricing page opens with an on-this-page index card listing every price group, so a phone visitor sees all prices in the first screen.
Closing dark panel with the knight crest, tap-to-call number and booking button; floating phone bar with a call button on small screens.

designs.concept: "The well-run shop." Everything on the page is an object from a good local business (the painted sign, the price board, the job ticket, the time sheet, the appointment card, the phone on the workbench), drawn on warm paper in ink, sign-painter's blue and Red Stick brick, with gold leaf only on blue. Light first; the dark theme is the same Baton Rouge street after closing, with the shop windows and street lamp lit.
signatureMoments: Hero: a hand-drawn SVG brick shop front (striped awning, iron balcony, 'YOUR BUSINESS' sign, work van) inside an arch, with the State Capitol tower and the river bridge on the horizon, a phone showing the missed-call text-back in front of it, and a round 'Fixed prices' seal stamped on. Switching theme cross-fades the street from day to night.

The story section 'What happens when a customer calls and you can't pick up': a five-stop route following one call, each stop shown rather than described (phone ringing on a workbench, the text thread plus the notification on the owner's phone, a booking dropping into a calendar, the enquiry list with follow-ups, the review request), ending in the example week as a time sheet.

The price board: the four fixed website prices in large Fraunces numerals on painted blue with a gold pinstripe, and the other prices as a dotted-leader price list. On the pricing page the same language becomes price cards (the 'Most popular' one under a scalloped awning), a payment-split diagram and menu-style ledgers.

Shop objects that replace generic cards: the four-step process as a job ticket with a 'You own everything' stamp, the three real projects as prints laid on a counter, Christian's business card, and the closing call to action as an appointment card (Cost: Free, Length: 30 minutes, Sales pitch: None).
The footer rises out of a Baton Rouge skyline silhouette (Capitol, downtown, the cantilever bridge), and the closing band has a scalloped awning edge.
fonts: Fraunces (variable, wght + SOFT axes, Latin, 62 KB, SIL OFL) for headings, prices and the brand name
Figtree (variable wght, Latin, 20 KB, SIL OFL) for text and interface

designs.concept: Your next move: the knight becomes the whole system. An 8-file board is the layout grid, the knight's L-shaped move is the only motion signature, and one signal coral always marks "the next move to make" (the square the knight stands on, the primary button, "Your move." in the headline). The offer is stated in plain words first ("More customers. Fewer missed calls." plus "Websites, automation and consulting for local businesses"), and the board beside it shows the product working (missed call, text back, booked, review) instead of decorating it. Ink navy chrome, ivory pages, the brand blue, Jost geometric display type.
designs.defaultTheme: light (ivory pages with an ink-navy header, hero and footer in both themes; a device that prefers dark gets the dark theme, and the toggle still remembers a choice)
signatureMoments: Hero board: a 4x4 corner of the board (files e-h) where the faceted knight hops in true L-moves from Missed call to Text back to Booked to Review; the coral track fills behind it, visited squares turn brand blue, the current square is coral. Rests on its finished state without JS or with reduced motion, pauses off-screen and on hover, and has a Pause button.

Services as a score sheet rather than a card grid: three ruled rows (Opening move / Next move / The long game), each with a chess piece on its own square in file a, under an a-h file ruler, with the fixed price in a coral-edged block.

Automation shown, not described: an L-shaped bento of HTML/CSS illustrations (phone text-back thread using the site's own '[your business]' message, a week calendar with a slot turning Booked, one enquiry list with day-2 / 1-week follow-ups and a review request), each labelled Illustration, plus the consulting page's example week as a real tally table with its 'example, not a measurement' note beside the numbers.
Process as four alternating ink and ivory squares in a rank (a 2x2 checker on tablet, a column on phone), followed by two plain assurances: you own everything, and one named person in Baton Rouge.

Typographic pricing: four ruled price columns in 64px Jost that fill ink on hover; on the pricing page, subgrid-aligned tier cards with an ink 'Most popular' card, grouped score-sheet price lists with a sticky heading, and the 50/50 split and Starter payment plan drawn to scale.
Small L-move details: a knight-move arrow on every 'go on' link that hops up-and-across on hover, pieces that make their move when a row is hovered, status chips that arrive by an L.
fonts: Jost variable (SIL OFL, self-hosted, 26 KB Latin): display, labels, prices, buttons
Manrope variable (already on the site, 24 KB): reading text

strengths: The only direction whose idea comes from the visitor's world rather than the designer's: a storefront signed YOUR BUSINESS with awning, van, street lamp, the Baton Rouge capitol and bridge. It says 'local, real, made with care' before a word is read.
Best phone first screen of the four at 390 and 360: Baton Rouge and the phone number in a utility bar, headline, lede, both buttons and the four website prices, all before the first scroll.
Best sticky bar: a labelled Call button beside 'Free 30-min call · no pitch', and at 360 it drops 'no pitch' rather than squeezing. It matches the order of actions in the brief.

Layout rhythm is the richest: icon strip, one wide card plus two, a five-step 'follow one call' timeline with a workbench drawing, a perforated time sheet, a job ticket with checkboxes, a blue price board, a business card, an appointment card, a skyline into the footer. No structure repeats.
Four or five real signature moments: the hero, the timeline, the price board with gold figures on blue, the appointment card ('Sales pitch … None'), and the night edition.
The dark theme is a second design, not an inversion: the same street after closing, with moon, lit windows and lamp.
Type is warm and confident (heavy soft Fraunces display, Figtree text) and body copy stays at 16 to 18px, the most readable of the four for this audience.
Colour has a rule and keeps it: blue is pressable, brick is 'notice this', gold only on blue.
weaknesses: Hero composition on desktop is crowded: the phone covers the lower left of the storefront, the 'EXAMPLE: WHAT YOUR CALLER SEES' pill butts into the shop sign, and the stamp sits on the arch edge. At 1280 the price strip under the buttons falls below the fold.
Mobile 'Website design & build' card: the phone mock covers the browser mock's title, leaving a stray 'usiness' visible at 390 and 360.
Longest home page of the four: 13 desktop stops and about 21 phone screens (15,364px). Automation is told twice (timeline, then time sheet) before work and prices appear; the price board is stop 10.

The pricing page falls back to stacked rounded cards (four tier cards with tick lists, four care-plan cards, an 'every plan includes' card). The price-board idea from the home page is not carried to the tiers, so the pricing page is the least distinctive part.
Restraint is the weak point: tilted project cards, tilted business card, tilted appointment card, two stamps, a scalloped edge and a skyline. A couple of props too many; it edges toward cute.
The staggered reveal on the care-plan cards is slow enough that the screenshot at pricing stop 6 caught the last card still faded.
assets/fonts still holds bricolage-grotesque.woff2 (131 KB) and manrope.woff2, which the stylesheet no longer references.

Fix the mobile website mock so the phone does not cut through the 'Your Business' title.
Cut the home page by roughly three stops: fold the time sheet into the timeline or move the price board up, and aim for 15 to 16 phone screens.
Redesign the pricing-page tiers and care plans away from four stacked cards (see the editorial spec table) and bring the price board onto that page.
Keep one tilted object and one stamp per page; straighten the rest.
Shorten the reveal stagger and delete the two unused font files.

strengths: The finest typographic craft of the four: Fraunces display with a blue italic line, Libre Franklin text, numbered chapters in a left rail, hairline rules, dot-leader price lists and a real scale. Type carries the page with almost no decoration.
Restraint: paper, ink and one blue. It reads expensive and trustworthy.
The hero shows the product (FIG. 1 phone with numbered markers keyed to four captions) and puts the phone number in the desktop header and under the buttons.
The big '200' numeral beside the example-week table with bars is a real signature moment.

The pricing page is the most scannable: tiers as a ruled spec table (LIVE IN / SIZE / DESIGN / AFTER LAUNCH), an 'On this page' contents list with prices, '50/50' numerals for payment, care plans as a table rather than cards.
Almost no card grids; sections differ in structure.
Phone layout is designed: step timeline, stacked price rows, sticky bar with label, call icon and Get a quote.
weaknesses: Pricing on phone is broken on the tier that matters most: the 'Most popular' Business block bleeds to the screen edge with no inner padding, so labels and ticks touch the left edge and '$4,000' is clipped on the right at both 390 and 360.

The register is an annual report: 'FIG. 1', chapter numerals, small-caps labels. Credible but cool; a roofer or salon owner may read it as a consultancy or law firm rather than a friendly local person. Baton Rouge appears only in the eyebrow and one trust cell.

Care plans as a table on desktop.
'On this page' contents list that shows each section's prices.
The giant '200 hours a year' numeral next to the example week, with bars for each line.

strengths: The strongest brand idea: the knight finally does something. The board is the grid, the L-shaped move links Missed call, Text back, Booked and Review, and coral always marks the next move. Nobody else's site looks like this.
The plainest statement of the offer: 'More customers. Fewer missed calls.' then 'Websites, automation and consulting for local businesses.' with the four prices in the hero.
A disciplined system: 2px corners, flat colour, no gradients or glows. Dark, but not generic dark SaaS.

Good rhythm: ruled service rows with chess pieces, a dark automation bento, the example-week table, an asymmetric work section ('Three live sites. Go and look.'), ruled price columns, a blue checker closing band with the crest large.
Pricing page emphasis is clear: the Business tier inverted to navy with a coral tab.
weaknesses: Concept ahead of audience: 'Opening move · Get found', 'The long game · Keep winning', file letters a to h and rank numbers are a designer's pleasure. A roofer does not think in chess, and the labels are noise.
Navy, coral and a geometric display face read as a tech agency. Nothing on screen says Baton Rouge or 'one person'. The hero is dark in both themes, so the first impression is a dark site either way.
The hero board is a diagram of four labelled tiles, not a demonstration; the phone conversation only arrives in the third section.
Headline leading is too tight: the descender of 'prices,' cuts into 'published' on both pricing headings, and 'packages,' into 'fixed'.
Hero headline runs over the board's first column at 1440 and stops a few pixels short of the 'Booked' tile at 1280.
Sticky bar has no call button, only a label and 'Get a quote'.
The four-step block alternates navy and ivory squares with large coral numerals; loud for what it says.
mustFix: Open the display line-height so descenders and ascenders never touch.
Keep the hero headline clear of the board at every width.
Remove the file and rank letters and the chess-jargon eyebrows, or cut them to one use.
Add a call button to the sticky bar.
Give the light theme a light hero, and add a visible local, human signal.
ideasWorthStealing: The plain second line under the headline: 'Websites, automation and consulting for local businesses.'
One accent colour reserved for 'the next thing to press'.
The headline 'Three live sites. Go and look.'
The crest shown large in the closing band.
The knight's L-move as the connector between steps (it could link the steps of the mainstreet timeline).

strengths: The best single demonstration: the hero phone plays the whole sequence (missed call, text back, reply, booked, review request) with a labelled stepper and a pause control, tied to floating missed-call, calendar and review cards.
'Miss the call. Keep the customer.' is the best headline of the four.
The hero lists the three offers with their fixed prices on the first desktop screen.
Each service row gets its own small interface vignette; the booking widget and lead list are convincing.
The deposit-split bar under each price is a smart small visual.
Components are consistent and cleanly finished.
weaknesses: The art direction is the modern SaaS landing page I have seen hundreds of times: Geist with mono uppercase labels, dot-grid background, peach and lavender glow, floating rounded cards, pill badges, 'LIVE' chips, glowing buttons. The dark theme is exactly generic dark SaaS. It fails the first criterion most.
It makes a one-person Baton Rouge studio look like a software product, to an audience that distrusts tech. Nothing local or human is on screen beyond the eyebrow.
The headline sells one $750 automation, not the studio; websites, the main line of business, are absent from it.
Small type: mono labels around 10 to 11px, row copy and price captions around 13px, add-on descriptions on the pricing page about 12 to 13px.
More repeated card patterns than the others: three equal project cards, four equal steps, four tier cards, bento cards.
The floating sticky bar lets page content show beneath and below it on phone, and at tablet width it is a narrow pill sitting on top of card text.
Little is memorable after the hero.
mustFix: Dock the sticky bar solidly to the bottom so no content shows under it.
Raise label and caption sizes and stop using mono for anything a customer must read.
Name websites in the headline or directly beside it.
Replace the generic dark theme with a designed one.
Add local, human signals.

verdicts.rationale: Mainstreet first, editorial second. Editorial has the finer typography and more restraint, and its pricing page is better built. But the brief's test is a roofer on an iPhone deciding in seconds whether this is a real, local, competent person, and mainstreet answers that on the first screen: Baton Rouge and the phone number, a storefront with his own sign on it, the four prices, a Call button in the sticky bar. Editorial answers a different question (is this a serious consultancy) in an annual-report voice with a lot of 12 to 14px type, and its phone pricing page clips the $4,000 tier at the screen edge. Mainstreet is also the only direction with an idea I have not seen before, and it has the most signature moments and the only dark theme that is a concept rather than an inversion. Its faults are fixable by editing: a crowded hero, a home page about three stops too long, too many props, and a pricing page that should borrow editorial's spec-table tiers. Strategy has the strongest brand system but serves the designer more than the customer; product has the best demo inside the most generic shell. All four pass the integrity checker with 0 FAIL, and none overflows horizontally at 360, 390, 820, 1280 or 1440. verdicts.rationale:
Judged as a non-technical plumber on an iPhone, mostly from the mobile sheets plus a 390px probe of each served site.

Mainstreet wins because it is the only direction where the first phone screen answers everything I care about without scrolling: where he is, a number I can tap, what he does in plain words, one obvious booking button, and the four website prices. Its sticky bar has a button that says 'Call' and a real booking button. Further down it looks like a local shop rather than a tech company: a brick storefront with my name on the sign, the Baton Rouge skyline, Denham Springs in the towns list, Christian's business card, and an appointment card that says 'Sales pitch: None'. I believe there is a real local person here, and I would be proud to have a site from whoever made it.

Editorial is second. It is the most readable and the most serious, with a very clear numbered phone figure, a phone number in the header and hero, and a first-person note from Christian. It loses to Mainstreet on three points: there is no website price on the first phone screen, the annual-report styling ('Fig. 1', lettered sections) feels bookish and not local, and the pricing page has a visible mobile bug where the featured Business card runs flush to the screen edges.

Product has the best demo of the four (the water-heater conversation that ends in a booking and a review request), but it never names the founder on the home page and looks like a software start-up, which is the opposite of the trust I need. Strategy states the offer plainly but wraps it in a chess gimmick, feels like a big-city agency, and gives me no way to call from my phone until the bottom of the page.

Recommendation: roll out Mainstreet. Fix its small issues (clipped chip row on mobile pricing, stamp crowding the hero phone, decorative checkboxes, unused fonts, home page length, restraint with props across 19 pages), and borrow Product's full-loop hero conversation, Editorial's numbered legend and spec-table price rows, and Strategy's bold one-line descriptor.

strengths: Cleanest measured result of the four. My audit found 0 contrast failures across 253-284 text runs per page in both themes at 1440 and 390, no horizontal overflow or viewport-clipped text in a 320-1920 sweep at 20px steps, zero layout shift, and no console errors at 360, 820 and 1920.

Lowest script risk. main.js has four small edits and is 20.4 KB, smaller than the baseline. All motion is CSS, plays once and never loops, so no pause control is needed; reduced motion leaves nothing running and nothing hidden.
Proper no-JavaScript handling: 12 html:not(.js) rules make the phone menu wrap under the bar and hide the dead menu and theme buttons. No content is hidden without scripts.

Real semantics. The hero illustration is a figure whose figcaption is an ordered list tied to numbered markers, so the story is available as text while the mock is hidden from screen readers. The example week and care plans are real tables with captions and scoped headers. Pricing has breadcrumb and on-this-page navigation.

The system suits the 17 remaining, mostly text pages: a 12-column grid with a left rail, ruled lists, dot-leader price lists (.pricelist, .rate, .leaders), a receipt (.slip) for calculator results and checkout, .field, .timeline and .toc. Few knobs: 3px and 6px radii, two shadows, one accent.
Colour is 96% tokenised with only 5 dark-only overrides. color-mix() is used only as an enhancement behind @supports with a plain fallback, so older phones still get a solid sticky header.

verdicts.rationale:
I put editorial first because it is the only direction that passes nearly every check I ran and its system is the one the remaining 17 mostly-text pages need. Judged on code, accessibility and robustness; audience appeal is weighted lightly here.

What I ran for each direction: the integrity checker (0 FAIL for all four, on the two pages and site-wide), the extra-width shots at 360, 820 and 1920 (no overflow or errors reported for any), and my own audit covering contrast in both themes, focus rings, target sizes, heading order, reduced motion, JavaScript off, a 320-1920 width sweep, and first-view weight. All four have one h1, no skipped heading levels, a working skip link, and zero layout shift.

Why editorial over strategy:
- **Measured defects:** editorial has 0 contrast failures in both themes, no overflow from 320 to 1920, complete no-JavaScript fallbacks and no looping motion. Its real defects are small: hero markers clipped at 360px, a weak form-field focus state, and a heavy italic font.
- **Strategy's gaps:** with JavaScript off the phone menu cannot be opened, and there is no tap-to-call in the sticky bar or menu. Both are short fixes, but its chess vocabulary and half-dark light theme are a design-direction risk an engineer cannot fix.
- **Fit for rollout:** editorial's ruled lists, left rail, dot-leader prices, receipt and real tables map directly onto FAQ, legal, process, contact, calculator and checkout. Strategy's tone-scoped tokens are the better architecture and should be ported into editorial.
- **Weight:** strategy is lighter (216 KB against 329 KB first view on the home page); subsetting or dropping editorial's 81 KB italic closes much of that gap.

Why the other two rank lower:
